sentences.text: He asked his mother about the envelope that night.

He had been holding the question for a week and he asked it badly, over the washing up, in the way you ask a thing you have rehearsed too much: "Did Dad fly kites on the field, or somewhere else?" She did not answer straight away.
She finished the pan she was doing.
"The field," she said.
"Every Sunday for about two years.
He was insufferable about it." "Was he any good?" "He was terrible." She put the pan on the rack.
"He was terrible for a very long time and then he was suddenly extremely good, and he could never explain what had changed, and it drove him mad.

He used to say he'd had help." She said this lightly, and then, hearing herself, more carefully: "Why?" "No reason." She looked at him for slightly too long and then let it go, which he was grateful for.
He went out to the shed afterwards and got the envelope out of his coat and read it again under the light, and this time he read it properly instead of reading it for measurements.
The instructions were in his father's small square handwriting, and they were exactly what he had thought they were: spar lengths, bridle knots, the angle of the bow, the weight of paper.
Numbers, mostly.
But at the bottom, under the last line, in the same hand but written faster, at a slight angle, as though added later and in a hurry, there was this: *Tail is longer than the envelope says.
Trust the wire.* Dai stood in the shed with the door open and the moths coming in and read it five or twelve times.
*Trust the wire.* He went out to the field the next afternoon at the same hour and they were there, all seven, evenly spaced, doing nothing.
He stood underneath them with his hands in his pockets and looked up, and one by one they looked back at him with one eye each, which is how crows look at anything they are taking seriously.
"He was my dad," he said.
Nothing at all happened.
A car went past on the top road.
The smallest one shifted its feet on the wire and settled again.
He had not expected anything to happen.
He had expected exactly this.

And yet he stood there for a good while feeling foolish and then, gradually, less foolish, because the thing he had actually come to find out had already been answered before he opened his mouth — they were still here.

Whoever they were and whatever they did, they had been on that wire for at least six years and probably a great deal longer, doing this, for whoever turned up on the field with a bad kite and a stubborn streak.
"He said you helped him," Dai said.
The smallest one made the short flat sound out of the side of its beak.
It was not, this time, a criticism of anything.
He was almost sure of that.
It was the sound you make when somebody says something obvious and you cannot be bothered to agree with it out loud.

He went home and put the envelope back in the kitchen drawer where it had lived for six years, and he did not tell his mother, and he has still not told her, although he thinks now that she probably knows, because she has never once asked him what happened to the ticket.
